subtype: Approach: clarifying what the mentee needs [Thinking]
passage:
Hi Seema,

Thanks for asking me to mentor you. Before I say yes to a plan, can I ask a few things? Where do you want to be a year from now? What has been hardest so far? I had planned to send you a list of technical topics, but after our call I noticed you hardly mentioned coding at all. You said you freeze in interviews and that three campus rounds went badly. So maybe what you need most is practice answering out loud, not more lectures from me. If you're up for it, we could do a mock interview next Saturday, and I'll ask you to send me two questions you dread. Tell me if that's not what you had in mind.

Anirban

qa.q: What did Seema say happens in interviews?
qa.a: Seema said Seema freezes in interviews, and three campus rounds went badly.

qa.q: What did Anirban believe Seema needed at first, and why did that view change?
qa.a: Anirban first planned a list of technical topics, but changed course because Seema hardly mentioned coding and talked about freezing in interviews.

qa.q: What could Anirban add to the mock interviews?
qa.a: Anirban could suggest Seema record the practice answers and listen back together, since hearing them helps show where the freezing starts.

qa.q: How might Seema feel on receiving this email?
qa.a: Seema would probably feel relieved and listened to, since Anirban asked before planning, though maybe nervous about the mock interview. 🙂

grounding: Shows a young engineer asking about goals and challenges before agreeing to mentor and realising that interview practice matters more than technical lectures.

subtype: Approach: clarifying what the mentee needs [Thinking]
passage: You asked how I started mentoring. A college student, Nikita, messaged me after my talk at her college, asking if I'd mentor her. I'm Elizabeth, four years into software work, and my first instinct was to plan lectures: data structures, system design, the works. Luckily, I asked her questions first. What do you want in six months? A job at a product company. What's hard right now? She said, 'I know the concepts. I freeze in interviews.' She'd cleared three written tests and failed three interviews. That changed everything. She didn't need me to teach her algorithms. She needed someone to sit across a table, ask her questions and let her practise out loud. So that's what we do now, every other week. Mock interviews. Honest feedback. She hasn't frozen in the last two.

qa.q: How many interviews had Nikita failed?
What was Nikita feeling in interviews?
qa.a: Nikita was anxious and freezing up, even though she knew the concepts.

qa.q: Why was asking questions first better than planning lectures?
qa.a: It showed that Nikita needed interview practice, not more theory, so the time went where it helped.

qa.q: How does mentoring look to Elizabeth now?
qa.a: Elizabeth sees that listening first saved weeks of the wrong help, and seems glad Nikita hasn't frozen in the last two.

grounding: It shows a young engineer asking a college student about goals and challenges before mentoring and finding interview practice matters more than lectures.

subtype: Approach: clarifying what the mentee needs [Thinking]
passage: I'm Siddharth, and I share a desk row with Sangeeta. Last month a first-year engineering student from her old college came to our office to meet her. I expected Sangeeta to open her laptop and start teaching; she's the best explainer on our floor. Instead she took him to the canteen and just asked questions for half an hour. What do you want to do? What's hardest right now? What have you tried? I could hear bits of it. He kept saying his English wasn't good enough for group discussions. By the end, Sangeeta had a list on a paper napkin, and none of it was coding. It was: speaking practice, one group discussion a week, and a mock interview in two months. I don't know what she felt. She looked thoughtful when she came back.

qa.q: What did the student keep saying?
qa.a: That his English wasn't good enough for group discussions.

qa.q: What might the student have been worried about?
qa.a: He seemed anxious and insecure about speaking English in group discussions.

qa.q: Why was the napkin list a better plan than coding lessons?
qa.a: It targeted what was actually holding the student back, speaking and group discussions, rather than skills he may already have.

qa.q: How might Siddharth see Sangeeta's choice?
qa.a: Siddharth expected teaching and was surprised by the listening, and may now see mentoring differently.

grounding: It shows a colleague watching a young engineer ask a college student about goals and challenges before mentoring and focusing on speaking practice over lectures.
